An architecture decision record (ADR) is a short note that captures one decision: why it was needed, what was chosen and what follows from it. Future maintainers should be able to read a record and understand the reasoning without asking the person who made it.
Write an ADR when a decision is hard to reverse, affects more than one system, or would puzzle a future reader. Do not write one for routine choices.

Each record lives in this folder as ADR-NNNN-short-title.md and has five sections: Status, Context, Decision, Consequences and Alternatives considered. Copy _template.md to begin. Status Meaning Proposed Written, under discussion Accepted In force Rejected Considered and declined Superseded Replaced by a later record, which it links to Records are never rewritten once accepted. Supersede them instead.

documents.t: The ecosystem needs a documentation site at docs.rjmlaird.co.uk that supports versioned documentation, search, diagrams and a custom domain, and that is cheap to run for a single maintainer. The services themselves run on Cloudflare Workers, but documentation is static content.
Build the docs with Docusaurus (with Mermaid and local search enabled) and deploy them to GitHub Pages using GitHub Actions. The docs hostname points at GitHub Pages through a CNAME record.

Hosting is free and tied to the repository. Deployment is automatic on a push to main. Broken links fail the build, which protects the quality of the site. GitHub Pages cannot set custom response headers, which limits security headers. There are no pull-request preview deployments. DNS is split between GitHub Pages and Cloudflare, so the domain model must document both.
To confirm: which alternatives were weighed at the time (for example another static documentation framework, or hosting the docs on Cloudflare). They were not recorded.

The planning inventory lists 34 candidate subdomains, many of which overlap. Each real subdomain brings its own DNS record, certificate, deployment and navigation. Search authority is split across hostnames. Because the session cookie is shared across *.rjmlaird.co.uk, every subdomain also sits in the same trust zone.

Create a subdomain only if it needs at least one of: a different runtime or build, a different security boundary, a different owner or audience with a distinct brand, or an external platform that requires it. Otherwise deliver the content as a path on the main site. Every subdomain must have an entry in the subdomain catalogue with a status before a DNS record is added.

Around 16 of the inventory hostnames become paths, and 5 are not created. One certificate, one navigation and one deployment cover most content. Some short URLs (for example cv.rjmlaird.co.uk) are lost unless a vanity redirect is added. Moving a section to its own subdomain later is possible, but needs redirects.

One subdomain per topic (the original inventory). Rejected: heavy maintenance, fragmented authority, and a larger shared-cookie surface. No subdomains at all. Rejected: the Workers services, docs and private tools genuinely need separate hostnames.
Recorded retrospectively This reflects a design stated by the owner. Deployment of both systems is not yet verified.
documents.s: ADR-0003: Separate the public API from the webhook services

documents.t: Two kinds of service are needed. One serves public portfolio data to anyone. The other handles commercial events from Stripe, Cal.com and HubSpot, and updates customer records. They have different audiences, different security needs and very different consequences if compromised.

Keep them separate. The public portfolio API lives in rjmlaird-api at api.rjmlaird.co.uk. Commercial operations live in the private rjmlaird-services repository, with webhook ingress at hooks.rjmlaird.co.uk. The services repository exposes no public portfolio data and no customer lists.

A flaw in the public API cannot expose payment or CRM data, because it holds none. Each system can have its own rate limits, secrets and release cadence. There are two repositories and two hostnames to maintain. Shared concerns, such as sign-in, are handled by auth rather than duplicated.
One combined API. Rejected: it mixes public and private concerns and enlarges the blast radius of any fault.

Provider webhooks enter only through hooks. No other service accepts them. A request is untrusted until its signature verifies over the raw body. The gateway holds webhook secrets and a queue producer, never storage or provider API tokens. Verified events are normalised into internal events; provider payloads are never passed on as they are. A redirect or client claim is never proof of an event. Only a verified webhook is. The contracts are in HTTP contracts and Internal events.

Version the URL (/v1/) for HTTP APIs and the type name (…v1) for internal events. Additive, optional changes stay in the current version. A breaking change creates a new version, and the old one is removed only after every consumer has moved. Consumers send unknown event types to a dead-letter queue instead of dropping them. Money is an integer in minor units plus an ISO 4217 currency, never a float. Validate every external input with a schema. Publish OpenAPI for any API with external consumers.

Several parts of the ecosystem run without anyone pressing a button: a documentation build on every merge, queue consumers that react to payments and bookings, and a planned daily wiki sync. This page lists them and sets out how new automation should behave.

Workflow Trigger What it does Status Docs build and deploy Push to main; pull request build check Typechecks, builds and deploys the docs Live (repository) Stripe event processing Verified webhook, then queue Records payment events In development Cal.com event processing Verified webhook, then queue Records booking events In development HubSpot sync Queue consumer Updates the CRM; HubSpot stays authoritative In development Client-delivery follow-ups Queue consumer Records a durable workflow once per confirmed payment and calls a handover adapter (the default adapter only logs) In development Wiki sync Daily schedule Pulls the chosen Notion page tree into D1 Proposed (architecture agreed) Zotero research ingest Request to /v1/research Stores library data in R2 under papers/ In development Local scripts (data parsing, metadata extraction) Manual To confirm To confirm

These are proposed standards for any new automation: Verify before trusting. Check the sender's signature on every inbound webhook before doing any work. Acknowledge fast, process later. Accept the event, put it on a queue, return quickly. Do the work in a consumer. Be idempotent. The same event arriving twice must not charge, email or record twice. Store a processed-event key. Fail visibly. Failed messages should land somewhere you will see them, not disappear. One authority per record. Never synchronise in both directions. HubSpot owns contacts; the automation writes to it. Run on a schedule only if you must. Prefer manual or event-driven triggers for the first release. The wiki starts with a scheduled pull and no webhooks.

Do any local scripts run on the owner's machine (for example for Zotero or metadata extraction), and what do they depend on? Each services queue has a dead-letter queue (see the webhook failures runbook). Who is alerted when one receives a message? Who is told when a scheduled job fails?

The domain architecture of rjmlaird.co.uk is intended to keep DNS small, predictable and easy to audit. This page records what is known about the current setup, what is inferred, and the rules that decide whether a new subdomain gets created. Status: Draft Only the docs hostname is verified from a repository. The registrar and authoritative nameservers are not yet documented. Treat everything marked inferred or To confirm as unchecked.

CNAME to GitHub Pages Repository README and static/CNAME How do Worker hostnames resolve? Cloudflare Worker Custom Domains Owner-stated for auth and hooks Is there a wildcard DNS record? Static content may live on GitHub Pages or another static host, while services live on Cloudflare Workers. DNS is the one place that holds the whole picture together, which is why it deserves its own documentation.

The planning inventory names www.rjmlaird.co.uk as the canonical web presence and rjmlaird.co.uk as the root domain. Proposed rule: pick one canonical host and permanently redirect (301) the other to it. Following the inventory, that means: https://www.rjmlaird.co.uk serves the site. https://rjmlaird.co.uk redirects to https://www.rjmlaird.co.uk, preserving the path. Trade-offs. Using www as canonical is the traditional choice and keeps the apex record simple. Using the apex as canonical gives shorter URLs and matches how the site is already referred to elsewhere. Either works; what matters is choosing one and applying it everywhere, including sitemaps, rel="canonical" tags and cookie scope. To confirm / technical debt The docs site currently links to the apex (https://rjmlaird.co.uk) in its navbar and footer, which contradicts the inventory's choice of www as canonical. Decide which host is canonical, then update docusaurus.config.ts to match. Record the decision in an ADR.

Lowercase, single-label, one purpose. For example docs, never docs-and-guides. Names describe a function, not a vendor. No subdomain without a catalogue entry. Every record must correspond to a row in the subdomain catalogue with a status and an owner. No wildcard DNS record. A wildcard hides typos and widens the takeover surface. (The shared session cookie is scoped to *.rjmlaird.co.uk, but that is a cookie setting, not a DNS record.) Remove records when retiring a service. A CNAME pointing at a deleted GitHub Pages site or an abandoned SaaS tenant can be claimed by someone else. Delete the DNS record in the same change that retires the service. Prefer redirects to new hostnames. A retired subdomain should redirect to its path replacement for as long as old links are likely to exist, then be removed.

Changes to the rjmlaird.co.uk ecosystem flow from a local machine, through an automated check, to production. This page documents the pipeline that is verified today (the docs site), the environment model planned for the Workers services, and the places where the two differ.

The docs repository uses pnpm, with the version pinned in package.json through packageManager (enable it with corepack enable). Node.js 20 or later is required locally. Local commands pnpm install pnpm start # live preview at http://localhost:3000 pnpm run build # production build; fails on broken links pnpm run typecheck # TypeScript check pnpm validate # typecheck plus build; what CI runs

The services repositories are pnpm workspace monorepos written in TypeScript. Wrangler runs Workers locally and deploys them; Vitest runs the tests. Exact local commands are To confirm and should be added to each repository's README.

The workflow is .github/workflows/ci.yml. Aspect Setting Triggers Push to main, any pull request, and manual dispatch Build job Checkout, pnpm setup, Node.js 22 with the pnpm cache, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, then pnpm run validate Deploy job Runs only on a push to main, after the build job succeeds Hosting GitHub Pages through the official Pages actions, with the build directory as the artifact Permissions contents: read, pages: write, id-token: write Concurrency One run at a time in the pages group; in-progress runs are not cancelled Two settings make the pipeline strict by design: onBrokenLinks: 'throw' and onBrokenMarkdownLinks: 'throw'. A broken internal link therefore fails the build, and a failed build never reaches production. Broken anchors only warn.

The docs workflow uses no repository secrets. It relies on the built-in token and the Pages deployment permissions. Environment-specific values belong in Wrangler configuration per environment. Anything secret never does.

This page sets out how assets are meant to flow between the asset services, and where public delivery stops. Little of it is built; the one confirmed use of object storage is a Cloudflare R2 bucket for Zotero files. Status: Proposed No cdn, dam or upload hostname is verified as live. The services are catalogued as planned; see the generated catalogue.

Service Responsibility Direction Access upload Accept and validate controlled writes Write Restricted Processing and approval Check, transform and approve assets Write Restricted dam Hold metadata, rights and approval; release assets for publication Write and govern Restricted cdn Deliver approved public assets Read Public, read-only dav Store Zotero attachments privately Separate Restricted
The write path and the read path share nothing except the approved asset that dam releases. cdn never accepts writes, and upload never delivers files.

Nothing is public until approved. An uploaded file stays unpublished until it has passed processing and dam releases it. Separate storage. Private buckets, including the Zotero store, never share a bucket, domain or cache rules with public assets. No uploaded content is served from the upload host. The shared session cookie makes every subdomain one trust zone; see Security, privacy and access. One direction. Assets move upload, then processing, then dam, then cdn. Nothing moves back.

The planning inventory recommended against dam and upload hostnames and for at most one asset host. The platform services plan supersedes that for the asset services. Record the decision and its mitigations in an ADR before moving any of them to active.

Good observability for a small ecosystem means knowing quickly that something is broken, finding out why, and telling the right people. Almost none of that is documented as in place, so this page is mainly a proposal and a list of questions. Status: Proposed No monitoring, error-tracking, analytics or status tooling is confirmed. Candidate tools below are options to evaluate, not decisions.

Capability Status Build failure notification for the docs GitHub Actions run status only Worker logs and metrics Cloudflare provides these for Workers. The services Workers emit structured JSON logs with request, correlation and event identifiers and redact emails and tokens; where the logs are read is to confirm Uptime monitoring To confirm Error tracking To confirm Public status page Proposed (status); no confirmed implementation Analytics To confirm

Each service should offer one cheap endpoint that returns whether it is healthy. The API template in these docs already sketches GET /status returning ok and version; adopt a consistent form such as GET /v1/status across every Worker. Each catalogue entry says whether a service is public. Only public services may publish a health URL, and restricted services' checks stay private. Never list internal health or monitoring URLs in public documentation.

Log events, not secrets or personal data. Include a request or event identifier so a failed webhook can be traced from provider to consumer. Keep retention short unless a legal or business reason says otherwise.

Host any public status page outside the infrastructure it reports on. A status page that goes down with the thing it monitors tells nobody anything. The page is curated: it reports a service state, drawn from the catalogue's public services, not raw metrics or logs. See status.
Alert on a small number of things you would act on at once: webhook failures, a failed scheduled sync, and the public sites being unreachable. Too many alerts will be ignored.

The full guide is Incident response. A pragmatic process for a single maintainer: Detect. An alert, a failed workflow run or a report. Assess. What is affected, and is any personal data involved? Contain. Roll back, disable a route or rotate a secret. Communicate. Update the status page if public services are affected. If personal data may have been exposed, consider legal reporting duties promptly. Fix and verify. Review. Write a short note. If the cause was an architectural weakness, record an ADR.
Is any uptime monitoring running? Are Cloudflare Worker logs enabled, and where are they read? Who is notified when a scheduled job fails? Is there any analytics on the public sites, and if so which?

This section documents the architecture behind rjmlaird.co.uk: the sites, services and infrastructure that make up Ryan Laird's personal, professional and technical web presence. It is written for four readers: the owner and maintainer, future collaborators and contractors, technical readers who want to see how the pieces fit, and non-technical readers who only need a mental model. Read the status labels The subdomain list that this section is built around is a planning model, not an inventory of running services. Every site and service carries a status label, and anything not yet checked is marked To confirm. If a page does not say something is Live, do not assume it is.

Label Meaning Live Serving real traffic today. In development Being built; not yet serving production traffic. Proposed Designed or recommended, but no build has started. Deferred Deliberately postponed until there is a concrete need. Includes exploratory ideas. Not recommended Considered and advised against. Recorded so the question is not reopened by accident. Deprecated Was live; scheduled for removal or already retired.

Each page also carries a confidence value in its front matter: Verified (checked against a repository or configuration), Partly verified, or Unverified (from planning notes only). Where a statement is inferred rather than confirmed, it is flagged inline.

The ecosystem exists to do five jobs: Present a clear professional and personal brand. Publish writing, research and astronomy and space communication. Sell and schedule services such as tutoring, mentoring and coaching. Explore ideas in public through experiments and data pieces. Run a small amount of back-office automation behind the scenes. In scope: the public sites, the services and APIs, the documentation site and the infrastructure that connects them. Out of scope: the internals of third-party platforms (GitHub, Stripe, Cal.com, HubSpot, Notion, Zotero). Only the integration points are documented here.

Status before subdomain. Nothing gets a DNS record until it has a catalogue entry with a purpose, a status and an owner. Paths before subdomains. Content that shares a build, an audience and a security boundary belongs at a path on the main site. A subdomain must justify itself (see the subdomain catalogue). Static first. Use a static site wherever possible. Add a Worker only where server-side behaviour is genuinely needed. Keep public and private surfaces apart. The public portfolio API and the commercial webhook services are separate systems. Private tools sit behind authentication. One brand system. global.css on the main site is the single source of truth for the visual identity. Other sites copy from it, never the reverse. Say what we do not know. Unknowns are written down as To confirm, not papered over. Prefer reversible, low-cost choices. This is a one-person operation; every extra moving part is maintenance debt.

Hostnames, visibility and lifecycle for every service are held in the canonical catalogue and published as the generated public service catalogue. Each service has a page under Platform services. This section does not repeat them.

Think of the ecosystem as a shop with four areas: The shop windows are the public sites: the main site, the docs, the labs and, later, space and research content. Visitors browse them freely. The locked doors are the sign-in service and the private wiki. Only the owner gets through. The back office is the set of small services that receive a payment or a booking, record it and update the customer record, without anyone pressing a button. The filing cabinets are the databases and storage buckets where those services keep their records and files.

The design shares one session cookie across *.rjmlaird.co.uk. This gives single sign-on across the ecosystem, but it has a consequence that shapes other decisions: every subdomain is inside the same trust zone. Any page on any subdomain receives the cookie. Practical rules that follow: Never host or serve untrusted or user-generated content on any subdomain. This is why upload must be restricted, accept programmatic writes only and never deliver what it receives, and why sandbox is avoided. Treat a compromise of any subdomain as a potential compromise of the session. Keep the number of subdomains small, and keep the cookie Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite-restricted. Prefer scoping cookies to the narrowest host that needs them wherever sign-in is not required. To confirm The cookie's exact attributes, its lifetime, and how an administrator is revoked from the allow-list.

Secrets are named in documentation but never shown. Store them as Worker secrets, set them from standard input, rotate them on a schedule and on suspicion of leakage, and never place them in a repository, ticket, chat, catalogue or generated file. Secrets are held as Cloudflare Worker secrets, not in repositories (the wiki's Notion token is the stated case). The docs workflow needs no custom secrets. Dependencies are installed with --frozen-lockfile in CI, so builds use exactly the versions committed. The services Workers hold their Stripe, Cal.com and HubSpot credentials as Worker secrets, split so that each Worker holds only what it needs (see the configuration reference). Rotation is documented in the secret rotation runbook. Not yet documented: who holds recovery access.

Topic Position Transport security HTTPS everywhere; see Domain and DNS model Docs response headers GitHub Pages does not allow custom response headers, so a strict Content-Security-Policy or Permissions-Policy header cannot be set there. A meta tag can cover part of this. The integrations in use process personal data: HubSpot (contacts), Stripe (payments), Cal.com (bookings) and the sign-in service (GitHub identity). The docs site also loads fonts from Google Fonts, which makes a third-party request from visitors' browsers. The following should be reflected in a single privacy page at /privacy on the main site and linked from every site's footer: What data each integration collects and why. Retention periods. How a person requests access to or deletion of their data. Which third parties act as processors. Whether any analytics or cookies are used.

Each service under docs/services/platform/ states whether it is public, restricted or internal, names one primary responsibility, says what it does not do and links to shared pages instead of repeating shared rules. Labels are defined in the architecture overview. Use them in tables as plain text, with the evidence in brackets where it matters, for example "Live (repository)".

Curly braces and angle brackets in ordinary prose break the build because Docusaurus reads .md as MDX. Put them in backticks or a code block.

This guide expands the process in Observability, status and incident response. It is written for one person acting under pressure, so each step says what to do first.

Stop the harm. Roll back a release, disable a route or revoke access. Prefer the quickest reversible action. Rotate anything exposed. If a secret may have leaked, rotate it now; see Secret rotation. Write down what you see. Time, symptoms and what you changed. You will need this later. Decide if personal data is involved. If it may be, treat the incident as serious and go to the section below.

Situation First action Public site down or defaced Roll back the last deployment; check DNS and hosting Webhook failures or missing payments Follow Webhook failures Suspected leaked credential Rotate it, then review recent use Unexpected access to a restricted service Revoke the credential or session, then review the access policy Dependency or build compromise Stop deployments, pin the previous known-good version and review the lockfile

documents.t: If public services are affected, update the status page once it exists. Say what is affected and when you will next update, not guesses about cause. Tell affected customers or partners directly when their data or service is involved.

If personal data may have been lost, exposed or altered, consider your legal duties straight away. Under UK GDPR, a notifiable personal data breach must generally be reported to the Information Commissioner's Office within 72 hours of becoming aware of it. Check the current ICO guidance before relying on this, and seek advice where unsure.

Within a few days, write a short note: What happened, and the timeline Impact, and who was told Root cause What worked, and what slowed you down Follow-up actions, each with an owner and a date If the cause was an architectural weakness, record an ADR and update the affected service page.

This is the proposed workflow for the data service. Publishing is a deliberate, reviewed act: nothing reaches the public service automatically. Status: Proposed No dataset has been published through this workflow yet. Adjust it once the service is deployed.

A dataset is eligible only if all of these hold: It is public, or you have the right to publish it Its licence permits redistribution, and you can state the licence and the attribution it requires It contains no personal, customer or private data You can name the source and the date it was retrieved

Record the source. Note where the data came from, its licence, the required attribution and the retrieval date. Prepare the data. Clean it reproducibly, with the steps kept in the repository, and define its schema. Validate. Check the data against the schema. Reject unexpected fields and missing required values. Describe it. Write the metadata: title, description, source, licence, attribution, coverage, update frequency and version. Review. A second look at licence, attribution and personal data before anything is merged. Publish a version. Release it as a new, immutable version. Never overwrite a published version in place. Verify. Fetch the published response and compare it with the source. Announce. Update the dataset catalogue and any affected documentation.

A correction is a new version. Keep the previous one available unless it is wrong in a harmful way. A breaking schema change is a new major version; see APIs and integrations. If a dataset must be withdrawn, for example because of a licence or privacy problem, remove it promptly, record why and tell known consumers.
Personal data, customer records, credentials, anything under a licence that forbids redistribution, or data you cannot attribute. See Security, privacy and access.

rjmlaird-services is the private repository behind the commercial side of rjmlaird.co.uk. It takes bookings and payments, verifies the webhooks that Stripe, Cal.com and HubSpot send, records what happened, keeps the HubSpot contact up to date and hands new clients over for delivery. It holds no public portfolio data; that lives in rjmlaird-api (see ADR-0003). Status: In development This section is built from the repository's own documentation. It has not been checked against deployed configuration. The service catalogue is still a placeholder, the intake forms are not connected, and several launch tasks remain. See the launch checklist.

A visitor chooses a service on the booking portal. Free sessions are handed to Cal.com; paid sessions go to Stripe Checkout through the billing Worker. Stripe, Cal.com and HubSpot send signed webhooks to service-hooks, which verifies each one and puts a normalised event on a queue. Private consumers record the booking or payment in D1, idempotently, and queue follow-up jobs. hubspot-sync updates the HubSpot contact (one way only). client-delivery starts a delivery workflow once per confirmed payment. Enquiry-only routes (focused reviews, teaching, speaking) deliberately have no automated quote-to-payment step. See Customer journeys.

Provider servers booking Service listing, booking intents and the portal pages at booking.rjmlaird.co.uk. Browsers billing Creates Stripe Checkout Sessions. Browsers stripe-consumer Sole consumer of service-events. Handles payment events and passes Cal.com events to calcom-consumer over an RPC service binding. Queue only calcom-consumer Records bookings and cancellations. Service binding only hubspot-sync Upserts HubSpot contacts from crm-sync-jobs. Queue only client-delivery Starts and records client-delivery workflows from client-delivery-jobs. Queue only Naming The repository is rjmlaird-services. The Worker behind hooks.rjmlaird.co.uk is called service-hooks. Despite its name, stripe-consumer also receives Cal.com events; it routes them to calcom-consumer.

The services system is a set of small Cloudflare Workers joined by queues. Browser-facing Workers are kept separate from provider ingress, and both are kept separate from the private consumers that touch storage. This page explains that separation and the delivery guarantees that follow from it.
The D1 tables are listed in the data model.

Public API (booking, billing). Browsers are untrusted. Routes and methods are allow-listed, CORS origins are explicit, request bodies are validated with strict Zod schemas and requests are rate limited. No stored data can be read through these Workers. Provider ingress (service-hooks). A request is untrusted until its signature verifies over the raw body. The Worker holds only the webhook secrets and a queue producer: no D1, no provider API tokens. Private consumers. No routes. They are reachable only through queues and one service binding. Private storage (D1 and queues). Never exposed over HTTP. D1 holds no card data, no raw provider payloads and no email addresses.

Each Worker is bound only to what it needs. Worker Queues D1 Service bindings Secrets service-hooks Produces service-events No No Stripe, Cal.com and HubSpot webhook secrets booking None No No None billing None No No STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, STRIPE_PRICE_* stripe-consumer Consumes service-events; produces CRM, delivery and DLQ messages Yes calcom-consumer None calcom-consumer Produces crm-sync-jobs Yes No None hubspot-sync Consumes crm-sync-jobs; produces its DLQ Yes No HUBSPOT_ACCESS_TOKEN client-delivery Consumes client-delivery-jobs; produces its DLQ Yes No None (adapter-specific later) Secret names and where to set them are in the configuration reference.

Queues deliver at least once, so every consumer is idempotent. webhook_events has a unique constraint on (provider, provider_event_id). An event already processed is skipped. Business state and the "processed" mark commit together in one transaction (D1.batch()). Downstream messages are enqueued before the commit. A crash can therefore duplicate a message but never lose one. Duplicates collapse through deterministic event IDs, the unique delivery_workflows.workflow_key and HubSpot's email-keyed upsert. Payments: checkout.session.completed and payment_intent.succeeded map to a single payments row. Delivery starts only on the first transition to succeeded. Messages that exhaust their retries go to a dead-letter queue (DLQ), one per queue. See the webhook failures runbook.

Any future admin UI or API belongs in its own Worker behind Cloudflare Access (identity-aware, with SSO and MFA), on a non-public hostname, reading D1 through a read-only binding or a dedicated service binding. It must not be added to booking, billing or service-hooks.

Customer portal (it needs verified identity; POST /v1/customer-portal-sessions returns 501). HubSpot inbound events (the webhook route verifies and acknowledges only). Reconciliation of payments to bookings (payments.booking_id is reserved). Booking reschedules.

Cal.com handles scheduling. When a booking is created or cancelled, Cal.com calls service-hooks, which verifies the signature and queues a normalised event.

Cal.com signs the raw body with HMAC-SHA256 using the webhook's secret and sends the hex digest in X-Cal-Signature-256. verifyCalcomSignature (apps/service-hooks/src/calcom.ts) implements exactly this and nothing else. Cal.com sends no timestamp, so replay protection relies on idempotency, not on a time window. Payloads carry no event id. The source event id is <triggerEvent>:<booking uid>. A rescheduled booking gets a new uid. BOOKING_RESCHEDULED is acknowledged and ignored in the MVP.

Condition Response Secret missing in production 500 webhook_not_configured Signature missing or wrong 400 Unsigned mode Allowed only when ENVIRONMENT is not production and CALCOM_ALLOW_UNSIGNED is true

HubSpot remains the CRM authority. hubspot-sync pushes contacts one way and never reads HubSpot state back.

Create a private app with only crm.objects.contacts.read and crm.objects.contacts.write. Store its token as HUBSPOT_ACCESS_TOKEN on hubspot-sync only. Create two custom contact properties (single-line text): rjm_booking_status and rjm_lifecycle_note. To use different internal names, set HUBSPOT_PROP_BOOKING_STATUS and HUBSPOT_PROP_LIFECYCLE_NOTE. Create the properties before the first job runs.

A crm.upsert-contact.v1 job maps to a contact like this. Nothing else is sent. Job field HubSpot property email (lower-cased; the match key) email First name firstname Last name lastname Booking status rjm_booking_status Lifecycle note rjm_lifecycle_note A job without a valid email or a lawfulBasis is rejected by the contract and dead-lettered. Flow: search by email, then PATCH if found or POST to create. If HubSpot returns an id, it is saved in provider_links against the booking or payment.

Condition Behaviour 429 Retry, honouring Retry-After 409, 5xx, network error Retry Missing token (operator error) Retry Permanent 4xx (bad scope, invalid property) Straight to crm-sync-jobs-dlq Backoff runs from 30 seconds to 10 minutes, with at most 5 deliveries before the message goes to the DLQ.

POST /v1/webhooks/hubspot verifies the v3 signature (X-HubSpot-Signature-v3, with a 5-minute timestamp window, using HUBSPOT_CLIENT_SECRET) and acknowledges. In the MVP it enqueues nothing. To confirm Only configure a HubSpot webhook subscription once an inbound use case exists.

Emails travel only in queue messages. They are never written to D1 or to logs (key-based and pattern-based redaction). Each job declares its lawful basis. The MVP uses contract for people who book or pay. Logs never contain emails or tokens. To confirm A deletion path (HubSpot GDPR delete) in the data-subject request process. How long queue messages, including DLQ messages that carry emails, are retained. Emails are absent from D1, but they persist in queues until retention expires. Which HubSpot app supplies HUBSPOT_CLIENT_SECRET, given that the contact sync uses a private app.
Stripe handles payment. The billing Worker creates Checkout Sessions, and service-hooks receives Stripe's webhooks. The signed webhook is the only proof of payment.

Subscribe the endpoint to exactly these three events. Event Handling checkout.session.completed Recorded when payment_status is paid. Otherwise (delayed payment methods) acknowledged and ignored. payment_intent.succeeded Recorded. Maps to the same payments row as the session. payment_intent.payment_failed Recorded as a failed payment.

In the Dashboard (Developers, then Webhooks), add the endpoint https://hooks.rjmlaird.co.uk/v1/webhooks/stripe. For staging, use the staging host in test mode. Select the three events above and no others. Reveal the signing secret and store it on service-hooks: Set the webhook secret wrangler secret put STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET --config apps/service-hooks/wrangler.jsonc Create a Price for each paid service. Set the matching STRIPE_PRICE_* secret on billing. These Price IDs are the purchase allowlist. Create a restricted API key with Checkout Sessions write access and store it as STRIPE_SECRET_KEY on billing. Secret names are listed in the configuration reference.

service-hooks reads the raw body once, as text, and checks the Stripe-Signature header (t=…,v1=…): HMAC-SHA256 over ${t}.${rawBody}, using Web Crypto and the endpoint's signing secret. Any v1 value may match, which supports secret rotation. A 5-minute timestamp tolerance. JSON is parsed only after verification. Failures return a generic 400. To confirm / technical debt This is a hand-rolled implementation of Stripe's documented scheme, chosen to keep the bundle small. It ignores the older v0 scheme. To use the SDK instead, call Stripe.createSubtleCryptoProvider() with constructEventAsync. Consider recording the choice as an ADR.

Stripe retries and duplicates events, so there are two layers of protection. Event level: webhook_events is unique on (provider, provider_event_id). Business level: the Checkout Session and its PaymentIntent resolve to one payments row, and delivery starts once. Session creation: billing sends Idempotency-Key: checkout:<serviceId>:<intentId>. A browser success redirect is never proof of payment.
Use test keys, a separate staging endpoint and stripe listen locally. Never mix live and test secrets in one environment. Use only Stripe's documented test card numbers.

To recover a missed event, open the endpoint in the Dashboard and resend the event. Resending is safe because duplicates are skipped. If a payment completed while ingress was down, resend checkout.session.completed. Check for refunds and disputes first; see When not to replay.

Event status overview SELECT processing_status, COUNT(*) FROM webhook_events GROUP BY 1; Events stuck for more than 15 minutes SELECT * FROM webhook_events WHERE processing_status != 'processed' AND received_at < datetime('now', '-15 minutes'); received for a long time means a crashed or retrying attempt. failed means the system gave up. Dead-letter queues. service-events-dlq, crm-sync-jobs-dlq and client-delivery-jobs-dlq. Messages are kept only for the queue retention period, so triage promptly.

Stop and investigate instead if any of these apply. Signature failures from an unknown sender. That is probing, not a lost event. A refunded or disputed payment. Check Stripe first. Replaying succeeded after a refund would start delivery for a refunded customer. A cancelled booking. bookings.status = 'cancelled' is terminal by design. Data past its retention window. Anything older than the retention or lawful-basis window for the contact. An unfixed fault. A deploy or configuration bug you have not fixed yet.

Consumers are idempotent, so a duplicate is skipped. That makes replay safe once the root cause is fixed. If it is not fixed, the consumer simply fails again. Prefer provider-side resend for missed ingress (for example Stripe's "resend"). It re-verifies and re-normalises the event, and duplicates are harmless. Re-queue a DLQ message only after the root cause is fixed. Replay in occurredAt order where it matters. Cancel-before-create is handled, but keep it tidy. Reset a stuck ledger row only with intent. Take a restore point and confirm the target first: Restore point (D1 Time Travel) wrangler d1 time-travel info <DB_NAME> Confirm exactly one row matches SELECT * FROM webhook_events WHERE id = 'evt_…'; Reset, then re-enqueue the event UPDATE webhook_events SET processing_status = 'received' WHERE id = 'evt_…';

Duplicates are expected and handled. A duplicate log outcome is normal. Duplicate side effects are a bug: two workflows or two CRM contacts. Check delivery_workflows.workflow_key and the HubSpot email search.
